title.narrative: Rural Upgrade of Resilience of Agribusinesses and Livelihood in South Sudan– (RURALSS)

description.narrative: 4,800 smallholder farmers organized in production and marketing groups.30 agribusiness cooperatives engaged in prioritized value chains.28,800 food consumers from targeted households.6,000 Children of school-going age in 20 primary schools192 Nutrition Role model mothers and male champions1,200 value chain enablers/actors

Specific Objective (SO)1: Nutrient-rich food availability in communities in South Sudan enhanced by end of 2026SO2: Nutritional status of households’ members in South Sudan improved by end of 2026SO3: Income of South Sudanese farmers increased by end of 2026

The RURALSS project is a 5-year grant (2021-2026) from the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands South Sudan. The project is a direct contribution to the post-conflict recovery of South Sudanese communities, building of strong agro-based livelihoods safety-nets, nutritionally sensitive and market-oriented farming system and sustainable agri-food system for better economic and nutritional outcomes. The project is directly implemented by AVSI foundation in collaboration with local authorities and private sector actors. The project implementation sites are in Eastern Equatoria and Lakes States in the Counties of Torit, Magwi, Ikwoto, Lopa, Cueibet and Wulu.

The project will deploy 3 main programming strategies namely:1 - Facilitation of smallholder farmers to engage climate-smart nutrition-sensitive agriculture, preceding production activities with knowledge and skills transfer using the Farmer Field Schools methodology.2 - Promotion of appropriate nutritional practices through social and behaviour change communication and awareness creation on CMAM (Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition)3 - Upgrading smallholder farmers and agribusinesses to higher nodes of targeted value chains through market-oriented value chain facilitative models (emphasis on value addition and product diversification) and inclusion of marginalized value chain actors

title.narrative: OP 1.1.1: Farmers trained in climate-smart and nutrition-sensitive agriculture (CS&NSA) approaches

description.narrative: County of smallholder farmers in FFS groups or cooperatives who attended at least 75% of planned sessions

title.narrative: OP Ind. 1.1.1: # of smallholder farmers trained in CS&NSA, leadership and governance

description.narrative: Count of smallholder who have been trained in climate-smart and nutrition-sensitive agriculture, leadership and governance

comment.narrative: In 2024, a total of 1,352 smallholders were enrolled across the project areas out of which 1,172 (473M, 699F) were able to attend at least 75% of the planned sessions on climate-smart and nutrition-sensitive agriculture, and leadership and governance. Participation was higher in Eastern Equatoria than in Lakes. Cueibet county had the least number of participants in planned trainings as many became ‘busy’ after receiving the planting inputs. This is despite earlier commitment to attend the planned trainings.

The targeted number to be trained is more than the targeted 2023 enrolment because 762 SHFs in 30 groups were carried forward from 2022 into 2023 because they did not complete their learning cycles in 2022.The achieved (2,688) exceeded the target of 2,262 because more SHFs were enrolled in 2023 due to high level of interest expressed by community members to participate in the FFS knowledge and skills transfer programme. This means the actual percentage that fully attended the knowledge and skills transfer is 81% (2177/2688) as some groups went dormant during the year. Leadership training was delivered to 219 group leaders. The current pace of achievement of the KPI is ahead of the project life pace for end of second year of 2,093/4,464 (46.9%).

title.narrative: SO3: Income of South Sudanese farmers increased by end of 2026

description.narrative: Increasing income level of households means they are able to have economic access to several needs of themselves and their households for which without money they are extremely vulnerable. Income is a direct resource that socio-economically empowers individuals and households to fend-off any stress or shocks to their wellbeing and growth of livelihoods safety nets.

title.narrative: SO Ind 3a: # of supported smallholder farmers and agribusinesses with at least 15% increase in net income from sale of agricultural goods and services (EKN FNS indicator)

comment.narrative: 1040 (54%) of project beneficiaries indicated at least 15% increase in their income from sale of agricultural good or services (mainly casual labour including cash for work) compared to 20% of the non-beneficiaries (control group). This increase in net income was indicated by equal number of male and female beneficiaries.

69% of the households that sold their foodstuff during 2024 indicated that their income levels had increased by at least 15%. The average yearly income from sale of foodstuff (including milk and animal meat) is €106 by selling 32% of the foodstuff produced by the household. Among the control group, 15 out of 25 indicated increase of at least 15% in income from the last year. This is indication that there is lucrative market for foodstuff as WFP exited most parts of the country not under emergency.

title.narrative: Goal: To contribute to the increased resilience of South Sudanese communities to shocks, to their nutritional wellbeing and socio-economic growth

description.narrative: The project aims to achieve outcomes that directly contributes to increased resilience of the communities in Eastern Equatoria and Lakes states as far as their nutritional wellbeing and socio-economic growth are concerned

title.narrative: Impact Indicator 2: # of households that demonstrated capacity to adequately manage shocks to their nutritional wellbeing and socio-economic growth (EKN FNS indicator)
Specific Objective (SO)1: Nutrient-rich food availability in communities in South Sudan enhanced by end of 2026

description.narrative: This outcome envisages that increasing availability of nutrient-rich foods will increase the resilience to shocks to nutritional wellbeing of the communities in South Sudan such prolonged periods of food scarcity/shortages

title.narrative: SO Indicator 1: Quantity of nutrient-rich foods (in metric tonnes) produced by smallholder farmers & agribusinesses (EKN FNS Indicator)

comment.narrative: In 2024, production data captured indicate that 1173 households (that were accessed out of 1,352 enrolled in 2024) were able to produce 1152.7 metric tonnes of foodstuff. This was 10.9% short of the 2024 target of 1,282.5MT. But the production level of 0.98MT/HH was above the target of 0.95MT. Ikotos county led in quantity of foodstuff produced with 515.8MT, followed by Magwi with 256.6MT. Wulu came last with 34.3MT. Cueibet output of 101.8MT could have been high had flooding not affected over 50 feddans of crops. It is important to note that this data excludes records from parts of Abara and Lobone payams in Magwi county as the HHs have been displaced from their homes due to the current insurgency in the area.

The project beneficiaries’ output of foodstuff produced tripled the target of 810 MT (0.54 MT per HH) for 2023, rising to 3,223.7MT (1.67MT per household). This is +2,263.7 MT head of the end of year project life target of 960MT produced by 2,250 HHs. This is generally attributed to the early adoption of recommended agronomic practices and provision of inputs by the project for engagement in production of 3 food groups. Production of cereals (1.07/HH) and tubers yielded the highest outputs despite still ranking below optimum productivities for the varieties supplied.

title.narrative: SO2: Nutritional status of households’ members in South Sudan improved by end of 2026

description.narrative: This outcome predicts that food consumers with normal nutritional statuses are in better positions to withstand stresses and shocks to their nutritional wellbeing for longer periods within which consumption smoothing or interseason bridging mechanisms are able to restore normalcy, thus rendering these food consumers resilient.

title.narrative: SO Ind 2a: # of household food consumers with acceptable food consumption score (EKN FNS indicator)

description.narrative: % of households in which FCS is acceptable (score of at least 35) over the past 7 days divided by all households that received nutrition-sensitive agriculture support and participated in SBCC activities

comment.narrative: 703 households were found to have acceptable food consumption score. This is less than the targeted 67% for 2024. The reason for this less achievement is that the consumption of fruits and vegetables is still low especially among the agropastoralists communities of Torit and Cueibet.

The second-year target was to have 900 HHs (40%) of HHs to have acceptable food consumption score (>35). The KPI survey found that 56% of the households had acceptable food consumption score. This could be attributed to the fact that the assessment was done during the harvest season and the fact that at least 850 HHs engaged in the production of foodstuff covering 3 or more food groups. Compared to the control group where 34% of the HHs had acceptable food consumption score, it is clear that the strategy to directly facilitate HHs to engage in production of 3 food groups coupled with rounds of nutrition education and food handling sessions paid off. But it should be noted that 35% and 8 percent of supported HHs still have borderline and unacceptable FCS respectively. Probably attributed to the high consumption of milk and the higher weight it commands compared to vegetables (more consumed in EES), the FCS of HHs in Lakes are better than those of EES with 69% vs 47% having acceptable FCS; 10% of HHs in EES have unacceptable FCS compared to 5% in Lakes.The fact that 60% of the control group household have borderline FCS means there is need to scale up nutrition interventions to more HHs within the project areas.The current cumulative achievement is 46.4% of project life target, which is ahead of the targeted of 28.1% expected by end of 2023.

title.narrative: SO Ind 2b: % of households food consumers with normal nutritional status

comment.narrative: CNAG members conducted routine screening of members of beneficiary households and in the process identifying cases for management. The project conducted two rounds of mass screening in March (1,534 persons) and November (2,025 persons) of whom 71% were U5s and PLW had their anthropometric measurements taken. These brought the total number screened to 7,818 (3,132M, 4686F). There was improvement in the number with normal nutritional status from 67% in March when screening started to 74.5% in November when the second mass screening was done. A 7.5% improvement. By sexes, the women (77%) had better nutritional status than the men (71%). Follow up investigation needs to be conducted to understand the reason for this 6% variation between the two sexes.*Worth noting that no control group was assessed because the communication arrived when the mass screening was already concluded.

The initial target was to screen only households enrolled in 2024, thus the 6,480 food consumers indicated in the target. But it was later agreed to screen households for 2023 and 2024 as well. This led to 16,607 (10,152F, 6455M) getting screened of which 13,664 (8,064F, 5,600M) were found to have normal nutritional status. This is 85% result compared to the 80% target set for 2024. It is an indication of improving nutritional status in the households.

title.narrative: OP 3.2.3: Transformative Bylaw for women inclusion in value chain governance and leadership formulated and adopted by stakeholders through roundtables
OP Ind 3.2.2 # of bylaw articles formulated and adopted

description.narrative: Count of bylaw articles that were formulated for women inclusion and were then adopted

comment.narrative: Communities proposed at least 12 bylaws during the roundtables conducted in 2024. On presentation to the payam authorities, some of them were merged leaving 9 bylaws that were signed off for enforcement. They covered control of movement of animals, regulation of utilization of water sources, peaceful resolution of conflicts instead of revenge killings, community participation in maintenance of roads and water points.

Roundtables were held in each of the payam of project implementation and the first resolution that was agreed upon was that of sharing leadership roles in community groups. It was agreed and adopted that the position of chairperson will be open to both men and women and once one sex takes the top position, the vice role will automatically be served for the other sex. It was also agreed that the positions of treasurer and secretary will be split between men and women members of groups. Current achievement of 12.5% is below the end of year two expected result of 3 adopted bylaws (37.5%).

title.narrative: OP 1.2.3: Peacebuilding dialogues conducted in farming communities
OP Ind 1.2.3: # of community members and stakeholders who participated in peacebuilding dialogues

description.narrative: Count of participants in peacebuilding dialogues

comment.narrative: The number of persons who turned up for the 15 roundtables that were conducted in the 5 counties was 613 (317M, 296F) compared to the targeted number of 300. This output is double the target for the year. It also enabled the project to achieve the project life target of 1,260 participants if the 2023 output is added to that of 2024. This is testament to the importance communities put to the need for peaceful co-existence and effective conflict resolution. The knowledge that bylaws are framed in the peacebuilding dialogues has been a key factor leading to increased participation.

The planned 15 roundtables conducted at payam levels to discuss GBV and Conflict-related issues attracted more community members than anticipated. High level of participation was realized (372M, 293F; 665, this is 52.8% achievement of project life target of 1,260 persons compared to 23.8% target expected by end of 2023. Women were given the platform to air out their challenges and risks they face due to gender-predispositions and stereotyping. One key resolution that emerged was the inclusion of women in leadership roles to increase their participation in decision making on issues that affect them and the entire community.

title.narrative: OP 2.1.1: Nutrition Education, Cooking Demonstration and Food Handling Sessions conducted
OP Ind 2.1.1: # of participants of the SBCC sessions

description.narrative: Count of participants of the SBCC sessions

title.narrative: Nutrition attendance sheet on Cooking demonstrations and SBCC mass awareness

comment.narrative: Many community members turned up for the nutrition education session, but the number was less than 50% of the target of 5,400 participants. Of the 1,792 attendees, 1057 or 59% were male. This is because the men wanted to see what their women are being called for so more attended. The projected resulted for end of 2023 is 30.7% but the achievement is 7.6%. During the cooking demos, the 735 females were the ones mainly involved in the hands-on processes while the men observed. Many men promised to allow their wives and daughters attend the subsequent sessions. Only 2 of the control group respondents indicated attending the nutrition education sessions, the rest indicated that they were no aware of the activity. It means better mobilization of non-beneficiaries within the communities is needed.

This is a community level activity that targets all members of a community. In 2024, the target was 5,400 participants to attend the planned 60 sessions (90 per session), The achieved output was 2,612 persons (across the 53 sessions conducted), which is 48.4% of the yearly target. But this represents an increase compared to the 2023 result. There has been a doubling in the participation of women (while the level of male participation remained the similar to that of 2023). The mobilization done on the radio and awareness campaigns are among the factors that led to the increased participation)

title.narrative: OP 1.2.2: School children engaged in mindset change activities to promoteclimate smart and nutrition-sensitive agriculture
OP Ind 1.2.2: # of pupils who attended at least 50% of food and nutrition activity sessions

description.narrative: Count of pupils who attended at least 50% of food and nutrition activity sessions

comment.narrative: Only 8 of the 18 targeted schools were engaged because the school management were undecided on working with the project. The enrolment target was not met in schools so the result is a true reflection of the reality. Current pace of 46% cumulative achievement is below the 75% target for end of year 2. In the 8 schools, both boys and girls were enrolled into the food and nutrition clubs. The project supported them to establish school gardens where they conducted practical activities and also cultivated fruits and vegetables. 61% of the pupils have indicated that they learnt new things in the field of food and nutrition, agriculture, and hygiene and sanitation practices. 32% indicated that they did not learn anything. 7% were not sure if they learn or did not learn anything from their involvement in the club. In schools where feeding programs are run, the club members have been able to cook their vegetables and consume during lunch to improve the diversity of their diets. Many have also indicated that they are applying the knowledge gained at school back home.

The project maintained 18 schools across Lakes and Eastern Equatoria states. New pupils were enrolled to join those who continued with the food and nutrition clubs totalling 1,119 (492M, 627F). More boys expressed intentions to join the club than the previous year as the work of the club has started to receive recognition from school authorities and community members. The pupils were able to set up vegetable gardens and fruit orchards with support from the project. Vegetables were able to reach maturity during the year, but the fruits will only start fruiting in 2 years’ time.

title.narrative: OP 3.1.1: Value Chain multistakeholders’ platforms established
OP Ind 3.1.1: # of supported smallholder farmers and agribusinesses actively participating in value chain multistakeholders’ platforms

description.narrative: Count of smallholder farmers and agribusinesses who are taking part in value chain multistakeholders’ platforms

comment.narrative: The participation of smallholder farmers, members of cooperatives and agribusinesses within the framework of Community Development Committees increased from 29% in 2023 to 85% in 2024. Through quarterly multistakeholder meetings held at CDC spaces attended by government official and other market actors, there is increased awareness and appreciation that scaling up of value chain activities required collective effort and innovations. Stakeholder have developed synergies, discussed commodity pricing, quality of inputs and market access, and committed their own resources to push some of their agenda forward like establishing more aggregation stores for commodities that require volume before offtakers commit their trucks to come and buy in bulk.

The participation of smallholder farmers, members of cooperatives and agribusinesses within the framework of Community Development Committees increased from 29% in 2023 to 85% in 2024. Through quarterly multistakeholder meetings held at CDC spaces attended by government official and other market actors, there is increased awareness and appreciation that scaling up of value chain activities required collective effort and innovations. Stakeholder have developed synergies, discussed commodity pricing, quality of inputs and market access, and committed their own resources to push some of their agenda forward like establishing more aggregation stores for commodities that require volume before offtakers commit their trucks to come and buy in bulk.

The project elected to use the PfRR framework to establish the multi-stakeholders’ platform. 15 payam-level CDCs were formed. 45 SHFs, 3 per CDC were selected and are actively engaged in the CDCs as representatives and link to other SHFs. The CDCs and the project have organized 7 market engagement days in which information regarding market opportunities, agribusiness and value chain opportunities and participation are disseminated. 328 project beneficiaries and 35 non-project beneficiaries have indicated participating in the platforms. Others have indicated that they had other pressing priorities so could not participate. Year 2 cumulative result of 16.7% is below the project life target of 46.5%.

title.narrative: IO 3.2: Utilization of value addition and enabling services by smallholder farmers and agribusinesses increased
IO Ind 3.2: # of smallholder farmers and agribusinesses/cooperatives engaged in value addition and product creation

description.narrative: Number of smallholder farmers or agribusinesses/cooperatives that are engaged in value addition and product creation activities

comment.narrative: 2 engaged cooperatives (Pekoyo in Magwi and Wulu Honey in Wulu) membership of 202 are the only ones currently engaged in product creation and value addition. Wulu honey cooperative processes honey and create products such as candles, propolis and wax for sale while Pekoyo engages in milling of maize into flour and making of simsim/groundnut pastes to sell to local communities. Other SHFs are yet to undergo training in value addition and product creation once they transition to agribusiness operations after completion of their learning cycles. Current cumulative achievement of 9.8% is below the end of year 2 target of 14.5%.

Achievement of this output is at 23.7% (213 beneficiaries – 154M, 59F), a low return mainly because many of the groups targeted for value addition support are not raising the required cost share (20% - 50% depending on the value chain) to fund the business plan. The project has decided not to facilitate a group until they have raised their quota of the cost share. Generally, the agribusiness mindset is lacking in many of the smallholders and even agribusinesses. They expect handouts from any NGO that approaches them.

title.narrative: IO 3.1: Enhanced access to lucrative markets for rural farmers
IO Ind 3.1: # of farmers and agribusinesses who sold or purchased goods through market opportunities identified by the project

comment.narrative: The target for 2023 was based on the assumption that at least 60% smallholders from 2022 cycles would transition to farming for markets in 2023. Unfortunately, less than 20% of the 2022 cohorts made than jump. This means many of the smallholders supported by the project did not have much to sell so could not be linked to markets due to lack of volumes. The 123 who were able to sell did so at events facilitated by the project such as the World Food Day Celebrations in Torit. Current achievement is 3% of project life target and way off the end of 2023 result of 47%. Much effort is needed in identification of market opportunities on one side and transitioning as many SHFs to agribusiness as possible.

The number of agribusinesses and smallholders who sold or purchased goods through market opportunities identified by the project is still lower than expected, 383 (182M, 201F) out of the targeted 1,300 SHFs. 2024 result was less than 30% of the target. The communities are yet to embrace structured market systems. Most smallholders preferred to sell within their communities and for immediate cash. They also dislike quality checks that they say reduce the quantity of their goods.

title.narrative: IO 2.2: Malnutrition management mechanisms strengthened in targeted communities
IO Ind 2.2: # of household food consumers with acute malnutrition successfully referred to case management points/service providers

comment.narrative: During the routine and mass screening 980 persons were found with different forms of malnutrition including underweight, stunting, wasting, and overweight. Of those 410 persons (229M, 181F) were found to suffer from severe and moderate acute malnutrition which are of interest for referral purposes. The project referred 318 (189M, 129F) for case management to service points the project has established working relationship with namely health facilities run by CUAMM, and treatment sites under UNICEF support. Only 162 (79M, 83F) or 51% of the referred cases reached the service points and received the required services. The rest had various reasons why they abandoned the referral process including having no food to stay at the facilities or the treatment centers being too far from their homes.

The CNAGs have continued to conduct routine screening for malnutrition. During the 2024 cycle, 2,943 (2,088F, 855M) were found with acute forms malnutrition that required referral to service points for care and support. Of these, 1,970 (1,390F, 580M) were able to access nutritional services. 973 were referred but did not access the required services due to absence of nearby service points to their vicinity or they chose not to seek the service due to belief that malnutrition is caused by spirits and so treated traditionally.

title.narrative: IO 2.1: Increased utilization of appropriate nutrition practices in households
IO Ind 2.1: # of households who have adopted nutritional and WASH practices recommended by the project

comment.narrative: 216 of the 735 beneficiary women and 2 non-beneficiary women who attended the nutrition education sessions stated that they are applying of some of the practices as follows: food handling and appropriate hygiene practices (87%), mothering infants and young child feeding (73%), food formulation for diversified diet (57%), early identification of malnutrition cases (44%), home-based fortification (43%). None of the males except the 54 nutrition male champions indicated transferring the knowledge or message to his households. This might also explain why there are higher incidence of malnutrition cases in males than females. The current achievement is 9.8% of project life target of 2,775 HHs and is less than the expected result by end of 2023 of 27%.

In the 3rd year, the expected result was that 900 households supported by RURALSS would meet the minimum requirements for good nutritional and WASH practices. Instead, 575 households were found to have met the set criteria for adoption of good nutritional and WASH practices. These represent 63.9% of the 2024 target. Reasons for this underachievement include deeply rooted cultural practices that the community members are reluctant to discard. Examples include the open defecation, drinking of raw milk, and poor food handling. Only 285 of the control group meet the stated minimum standards

title.narrative: Intermediate Outcome (IO) 1.2: Broadened scope of engagement of smallholder farmers and agribusinesses in agri-food value chains (crops, livestock, fisheries, agroforestry)
IO Ind 1.2a: # of smallholder farmers engaged in value chains that cover at least 3 food groups

description.narrative: Count of smallholder farmers engaged in value chains that cover at least 3 food groups *food groups are 1) cereals/sugars, 2) meat (beef, fish, poultry, pork), 3) milk and eggs, 4) legumes/pulses/oil seeds, 5) fruits and vegetables, 6) condiments (spices, coffee, tea

comment.narrative: Out of the 1,352 SHFs who received inputs for engaging in nutrition-sensitive agriculture, 989 (388M, 601F) cultivated crops that covered at least 3 food groups to take care of bodybuilding, energy-giving and protective foods. This is 73.1% of those facilitated and meets the target of 900 that was set for 2024. Maize comprised 46% of the crops cultivated, followed by sorghum at 28%, then groundnuts at 22% and the rest 4%. Production of horticultural crops is still at a low level, at less that 3% of the production in households. Those who did not meet the targeted attributed it to prolonged dry spell that discouraged them from engaging in many enterprises and others are still not keep on vegetable production as they consider their consumption as a sign of poverty life. Among the non-project smallholders, 48% cultivate crops/rare animals covering at least 4 food groups.

The target was 90% but achievement registered was 63% (850 HHs instead of 1,350). This is because almost 100% of households cultivate cereals and pulses but are reluctant to engage in vegetable growing especially in Lakes state where consumption of vegetables is regarded a sign of poverty. In Eastern Equatoria, many households were interested in horticultural crops, but the dry spell discouraged many. Those who managed to engage had access to water points for their fields. Livestock farming in Lakes contributed to this indicator as over 300 households engaged in milk production for consumption in their households. The project is at 29% against an anticipated pace of 46.9% of project life target at end of 2023.

title.narrative: OP 3.2.1: Smallholder farmers and agribusinesses accessed financial credit through VSLAs and financial institutions
OP Ind 3.2.1: # of smallholder farmers participating in VSLAs

description.narrative: Count of smallholder farmers who take part in VSLAs

comment.narrative: The percentage of SHFs saving by the 2024 VSLA cohort reduced compared to 2023 as only 88.2% (1,192 out of 1,352) committed to saving in the 56 groups that remained functional. 4 groups in Torit outright rejected to save if the project did not give them the money to save. The 56 groups were able to save $28,626 during their cycle, averaging $511 per group.

VSLA is included as compulsory in the selection criteria for membership to Farmer Groups. All groups were trained in the VSLA methodology and availed with VSLA kits to conduct the savings. The project registered a 115% achievement as there are 2,604 SHFs in the FGs than 2,262 planned for. Current achievement of 54.3% is above the 2023 project life target of 46.9%.

title.narrative: Intermediate Outcome (IO) 1.1: Increased climate-smart and nutrition-sensitive agriculture (CS&NSA) knowledge and skills of smallholder farmers and agribusiness owners
IO Ind 1.1b: # of hectares of farmland per household under atleast 3 CSA approaches (EKN FNS indicator)

comment.narrative: The target for 2023 was for each household to use at least 2 feddans (0.84ha) for cultivation. End of season assessment show that each household utilized 0.4 feddans for the cultivation of foodstuff using inputs mobilized by themselves and those provided by the RURALSS project. This result is below the project target. The project plan to facilitate land opening so that acreage used per household can go up.

There has been improvement in both the acreage cultivated at HH level and application of climate smart agriculture approaches. The main approaches applied have been the cultivation of drought-resistant crop varieties, mulching using organic matter, digging canals through and around crop fields, watering of horticultural fields using watering cans and where possible hosepipes where small-scale irrigation is practiced. Out of the 1,352 SHFs directly supported by the project, 1000 (380M, 620F) applied at least 3 CSA approaches to 764.3 hectares of land. A slight increase from the 2023 achievement (0.4Ha in 2023 to 0.567Ha in 2024 per HH). Nevertheless, this was below the target of 1.26Ha set for 2024. Households are responding slowly to increasing acreage of land used for cultivation and application of CSA approaches. In the control group, at least 3 CSA approaches in applied in 0.3Ha per HH. The project beneficiaries fared better.

title.narrative: OP 1.2.1: Farmers, agripreneurs and cooperatives accessed quality inputs and adequate enabling services to facilitate their engagement in nutrition-sensitive value chains activities
OP Ind 1.2.1: # of smallholder farmers, cooperatives members who received agricultural inputs for engagement in CS&NSA and extension services

description.narrative: Count of smallholder farmers who are part of FFS or cooperatives who received agricultural inputs that include planting materials, farming tools, post-production handle equipment, etc for engagement in CS&NSA and extension services

comment.narrative: 1926 beneficiaries from 2023 enrolment and 762 carried forward from 2022 received inputs to engage in nutrition-sensitive and climate smart agriculture. Important to note that those carried forward from 2022 only received seeds to cultivate foods that cover at least 3 food groups. They did not receive tools because they had already received them in 2022. The project coverage with inputs is at 56% compared to the project life pace of 46.9% by the end of 2023.

All the 1,352 (546M, 896F) enrolled smallholder farmers (those who are members of cooperative societies in Wulu, Magwi and Cueibet) received seeds and tools for production of foodstuff. Project staff and payam extensions workers provided technical assistance that the SHFs required. Each household received 5kg pack of a cereal (maize or sorghum), 2kgs of pulses (groundnuts or beans), 2 sachets of vegetable seeds (any 2 of their preference – that included tomatoes, spinarch, collards, cabbages, eggplants, onions, carrots and okra). Households that were ready (had prepared lots for fruit growing) received 200 assorted fruit tree seedlings each.

With the aim of supporting the local seed system, AVSI selected one of its prequalified input dealers (Magwi Seed Company – MASCO) to supply agricultural inputs to all the 762 SHFs (330M, 432F) of the 30 farmer groups that were engaged in 2022. The inputs included an assortment of farming tools such as ox ploughs, hand hoes, watering cans and strings. The seeds that each group received was determined by the choice of study and commercial enterprises that they had picked. It is important to note that only not all groups that received inputs utilized them. Many SHFs opted out of engaging in production activities late in the year due to genuine fear of season failure.

title.narrative: Community Nutrition Action Group (CNAG) formation

comment.narrative: .In 2024, an additional 135 CNAG members were trained and equipped to conduct routine surveillance of malnutrition, delivery nutrition education and run cooking demonstration. This target was achieved 100% and the CNAG colleagues are fully engaged in the various project activities and tasks assigned to them. The CNAG model is highly appreciated by local authorities. This is due to their efficiency in early detection of malnutrition cases and support of the referral process as well as the increasing awareness on good nutritional and hygiene practices within the communities.

The project formed 18 CNAGs but maintained 15 (as the 3 in Lopa Lafon were out of reach). In the 15 groups there are 162 members of which 54 are nutrition male champions and 108 are role model mothers. These members underwent 3-day training in their respective counties facilitated by project nutrition and State Ministry of Health staff. After the training they were equipped with IEC materials, personnel protection equipment branded with nutrition and WASH messages and each group provided a bicycle to facilitated movements during community mobilization and holding sessions. The project achievement of establishing CNAGs stand at 67.9% compared to expected end of year 2 project life result of 40%
